images.caption: Figure 1:Teaser.World Observer jointly generates panoramic observers with the actor. (a) Decoupled observer enables control over actor’s unseen regions. (b) Multiple observers can be placed flexibly to track occluded regions.

Figure 2:Motivation.When dynamic objects leave the actor’s view, existing models exhibit four failures: (a) frame-locked, (b) lost, (c) frozen, and (d) impostor state. These failures show the difficulty of maintaining and evolving states without direct observations during out-of-view intervals.

Figure 3:Dataset Overview.Real-world (top) and synthetic (bottom) examples with moving and two-fixed-observer configurations, respectively. Colored boxes show cross-view correspondences, while the rightmost diagrams show camera configurations and trajectories.

Figure 4:Model Overview.(a) World Observer jointly generates actor and panoramic observer streams with a shared DiT.
(b) Observer Sink converts the high-resolution initial panorama into four perspective references for fine-grained appearance.

Figure 5:Visualization of self-attention.A query on a re-entering object attends to the observer region holding its out-of-view state, while the object fails to re-enter after out-of-view interval in non-joint model (Baseline).
Figure 6:Qualitative results.World Observer supports (a) state memory, (b) observer-prompted control, (c) long-horizon generation, and (d) multi-observer. Insets show the observer views.

Figure 7:Qualitative comparisons with other models.Red boxes mark target objects before exit and after re-entry. While existing models often lose, freeze, or inconsistently reconstruct them, World Observer better preserves object identity and state evolution across out-of-view intervals.

Figure 8:Out-of-view dynamics evaluation protocol.We track dynamic objects in 3D to evaluate their exit and re-entry (OOV-F) and motion consistency during out-of-view intervals (OOV-Dself{}_{\text{self}}and OOV-Dgt{}_{\text{gt}}).

Figure 9:Comparison with existing Out-Of-View metrics.VLM-based metrics fail to identify frozen and impostor states as inconsistent, while our 3D displacement-based metrics quantitatively capture these failures.

Figure 10:Additional qualitative comparisons with other models.We provide additional comparisons of World Observer with existing world models on real and synthetic scenes involving out-of-view dynamics. For synthetic scenes, we additionally include results from World Observer (Multi). Red boxes highlight the target objects before exit and after re-entry. Across diverse objects, motions, and scenes, existing models exhibit out-of-view failures such as lost, frozen, and impostor states, whereas World Observer consistently preserves object identity and state evolution throughout the out-of-view interval.

Figure 11:Qualitative ablation results.We show the effect of removing each component on generation quality. Without the observer, the model fails to maintain out-of-view dynamics, causing the dynamic object to disappear when it re-enters the view. Without the actor, panorama-based generation followed by cropping leads to reduced visual fidelity. World Observer preserves evolving out-of-view dynamics while maintaining high-fidelity generation.

Figure 12:Qualitative ablation results in AR generation.We compare ground truth with variants without the observer and Observer Sink under a long camera trajectory with a full360∘360^{\circ}sweep.
Without the observer, out-of-view object dynamics are not maintained, while removing the Observer Sink degrades fine appearance under large viewpoint changes.
Our full model preserves both dynamic objects (red/yellow) and appearance details (green) upon re-entry.

Figure 13:Qualitative prompt ablation results.We compare (a) actor-concentrated, (b) unified, and (c) decoupled actor-observer prompting.
Actor-concentrated prompting misplaces off-view events in the actor view, while unified prompting can hallucinate duplicate subjects in the observer.
Decoupled prompting instead produces a consistent event across both streams.
